before:
You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you've been staring at the rug. I count that as pl/ork too, even if it feels like it's in the way. Before you decide where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or what it wants. Maybe it just has something to say. It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. Maybe it's that parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.

You won't always know which, but a fear that keeps coming back to tell you something is worth talking to as a part of you either way. Use as little of this picture of your insides as still helps you. A sentence that crosses your mind once might just be thinking, and so might the same worried question coming back for another answer. You can let those go and come back to the room you're in. If it sounds like your little one, though, listen to it the first time.

I wouldn't spend long deciding what to call each one, though. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that's trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn't have to get any louder. That part learns it has to shout when nobody listens, or when the inherited critic voice makes fun of it.

If you push past a reaction, the part of you behind it can learn that you still don't listen when it says no. You could tell it something like, "I see you. I'm not going to force my way past you. What's going on?" Or however you'd actually say that. Then wait. Don't grill the silence, and if nothing comes, don't answer for that part just because you'd set this up as a healing session.

guide_passage: If nothing speaks, notice its triggers, bodily effects, and what it makes you do or avoid. An apparent protective purpose is a hypothesis: what it is trying to prevent and what it actually prevents are separate questions. A voice, intuition, or presence can offer information without taking the steering wheel. Is its guidance loving, wise, helpful, and freedom-preserving? Those are tests for following advice, not conditions for allowing difficult feelings to be heard.
next:
Two patterns often do have a protective function. 
Proactive protection
 stays on duty most of the time: the skeptic, intellectualizer, inner critic, or voice watching for weakness and self-indulgence. It may have spent years preventing humiliation, deception, overwhelm, or another abandonment. It has probably watched you begin other healing methods with great enthusiasm and then disappear. It may be tired, but it is experienced and competent.
length: four to six sentences, 70 to 120 words
brief:
- the last paragraph of "Start With Whatever Showed Up" before its first h3, right after the paragraph that ends "if nothing comes, don't answer for that part just because you'd set this up as a healing session."
- what it has to carry, in meaning: if nothing answers, you can still watch the reaction itself, like what sets it off and what it does in your body or makes you do (if you keep three of these, give each its own sentence). What the reaction seems to be protecting you from is only a guess: what it's trying to prevent and what it actually prevents can be two different things. Something might come, though, as a voice or a hunch, and it can tell you something without taking over. Follow its advice only if it's loving and leaves you free (the guide also asks whether it's wise and helpful; you don't need every test), and when it pushes toward something big or hard to undo, see whether it still looks right once you're calm and against what has actually happened (if you're in danger, get safe first). Those tests are only for advice. What comes might be a feeling, like grief or anger, and a feeling gets heard whether it passes them or not.
- Say "the reaction" where you mean the reaction. In turn 19 the cold reads couldn't tell whether "it" was the reaction, the voice or a feeling, and they couldn't place "a hard feeling" that nothing had set up.
- In turn 19 every draft strung the guide's lists through its sentences, three or four lists each, and the one checked was 100% AI.
- No list of three or more in one sentence (Joel, 2026-10-03: "lists of 3 in general are an ai pattern"). If a list doesn't need all its items, keep the one or two that matter most; if every item matters, give each its own sentence.
- Don't open with the brief's words. The order is yours: start from what the reader was just told (nothing may come) or from what might come instead, whichever reacts better to the paragraph before.
- The article already has, in You Don't Need an Inner Monologue: "Maybe what's actually requiring your attention now is a knot in your stomach." Don't repeat it. It also has "if they've actually hurt or threatened you, even once, old stuff or not, get safe first", so the danger case is a few words, not a lesson. No steering wheel or driving picture, and no "gets to" or "get to" for the voice.
- Every sentence has to work for a reader who doesn't remember anything sections back; core terms (your little one, the Nurturer, the Protector, the Guide, the inherited critic voice, borrowed adulthood, pl/ork) are fine.
